prime.problem: LLMs miscount letters, fumble arithmetic, cost more in Korean, and derail on a stray space or a strange word. Without knowing what the model actually receives, these look like random flaws of "intelligence" that you can't predict or work around.
prime.fits: This is the payoff of the whole lecture. You've built BPE, the regex pre-split, special tokens and the vocab-size trade-off; now each of Karpathy's opening list of weird behaviours gets traced back to one of those pieces.
expect: the tokenizer's training data vs the LLM's
prime.goal: Look at a strange LLM failure, print the token ids, and name which tokenization cause produced it and what to change.

attend: Why can a model that has read millions of words still not see the ls in DefaultCellStyle?
Which quirks come from what the tokenizer was trained on, and which from where the prompt cuts a token?
Why does a prompt ending in a space push the model somewhere it has rarely been?
How can a token be in the vocabulary yet have an embedding row that never learned anything?
Which fixes in GPT-4's tokenizer (space runs, 3-digit numbers) remove a quirk, and which quirks remain?

must: The model's input is token ids, not characters → a long token like .DefaultCellStyle (98518) is one embedding row → its letters aren't in the input → spelling, counting and reversal fail unless the text is first spelled out one letter per token

BPE merges follow the tokenizer's training text → frequent text (English, common digit pairs) gets long tokens, rare text (Korean) gets short ones → more tokens for the same meaning and digit chunks that don't line up with place value → bloated context and shaky arithmetic

The tokenizer and the LLM are trained on different data → a token frequent in the first but absent from the second (␣SolidGoldMagikarp, 43453) never appears in a batch → its embedding row gets no gradient → feeding it gives the model a vector it never learned to read

The space usually belongs to the next token (␣Oh = 8840) → a prompt ending in a lone 220, or cut mid-token (DefaultCellSta), is a sequence the model rarely saw in training → strange continuations or an immediate stop
elevated: Special tokens are matched as strings before BPE → if user text is parsed for them, typing <|endoftext|> inserts the real id 50256 → so tiktoken refuses by default and you opt in with allowed_special
reference: the JSON vs YAML token counts for any one record

compress.prompt: From memory, sort Karpathy's quirks into three causes and name one example of each. Then, in 3–4 sentences, explain why SolidGoldMagikarp breaks the model while a merely rare word does not.
checklist: cause 1: a token hides its characters (spelling, reversal, arithmetic)
cause 2: the tokenizer's training text sets what is cheap or even present (non-English, GPT-2 Python, YAML vs JSON, SolidGoldMagikarp)
cause 3: the prompt breaks a token boundary (trailing space, partial token, <|endoftext|>)
a rare word splits into common, well-trained tokens; a glitch token is one id whose row got no gradient
the fix is usually in the text or the tokenizer settings, not the model

retrieve.q: Explain why an LLM can fail to count the letters of a word it can use perfectly well in a sentence.
answer: the word may be one token, so the model receives one id, not its letters
using the word only needs its meaning; counting needs its spelling, which must be memorised per id
spelling it out with spaces gives one token per letter (16 tokens for DefaultCellStyle)

retrieve.q: Walk through what happens when a user prompt ends with a space: what the tokenizer emits, what the model has usually seen at that position, and what it has to produce next.
answer: the prompt ends in the lone space token 220
in training, a space after : almost always came glued to the next word (␣Oh = 8840)
the model must now continue with a space-less token (Oh = 12174) after a bare 220, a rare pattern
result: worse or odd completions, hence the warning

retrieve.q: Walk through how ␣SolidGoldMagikarp ended up as one GPT-2 token whose embedding is useless.
answer: it was frequent in the tokenizer's training text (a Reddit username), so BPE merged it into id 43453
the LLM's training text didn't contain it, so id 43453 never appeared in a batch
embedding rows only get gradient from tokens in the batch, so the row stayed as initialised
at inference the model reads an untrained vector

retrieve.q: You're choosing a tokenizer for a new model that must do arithmetic and serve Korean users. What would you take from GPT-4 and Llama 2, and what does each choice cost?
answer: numbers: cap chunks at 3 digits (GPT-4) or split every digit (Llama 2's split_digits); digits give consistent place value but longer sequences
Korean: include enough Korean in the tokenizer's training text so it earns merges, at the cost of vocabulary slots for other text
a bigger vocabulary shortens sequences but grows the embedding and lm_head
keep the tokenizer's and the LLM's training data aligned to avoid untrained tokens

compare.q: The tour showed odd splits (numbers, Egg/egg, Korean, indents); this card explains the resulting behaviours. For the number splits, what is the observation, what design choice causes it, and how did GPT-4's tokenizer change the failure rather than remove it?
answer: observation: 677 is one token but ␣677 is ␣6|77
cause: BPE merges frequent digit pairs, with no notion of place value
GPT-4's regex caps chunks at 3 digits and splits off the space, so 4-digit numbers always go 3+1
consistent, but still not aligned with columns; per-digit splitting (Llama 2) is the stronger fix

compare.q: Adding a new token by model surgery vs a SolidGoldMagikarp-style glitch token: both start with an untrained embedding row. What makes one useful and the other harmful?
answer: surgery: you add the row and train on data containing it, so it gets gradient (only row 50257 did in the lab)
glitch token: the row exists but the LLM's data never contains the token, so it never trains
failure mode of surgery: too little fine-tuning data leaves the new row near its initialisation, the same problem at a smaller scale

predict.q: GPT-2 spends a token on almost every indent space. If your Python used tabs instead of 4 spaces, predict how many GPT-2 tokens \t\tprint(i) takes compared with print(i) (8 spaces), and what else changes about the print token.
predict.answer: 6 tokens vs 11. Each tab is one token (197), while 8 spaces become seven 220s with the eighth space glued to ␣print (3601). The catch: after a tab there is no space to glue on, so print becomes a different id (4798). The same keyword now has two ids depending on the indent style, and the model must learn both. Computed with tiktoken's gpt2 encoding.

apply.task: Diagnose with token ids, not guesses. Using tiktoken's cl100k_base, encode DefaultCellStyle, its reverse elytSlleCtluafeD, and the spaced-out form D e f a u l t C e l l S t y l e. Then loop over range(1000, 10000) and count how gpt2 splits each number (as digit lengths per token).
apply.done: You get 1, 8 and 16 tokens for the three strings, and the gpt2 tally 2+2: 5,807 · 1+3: 2,538 · 3+1: 538 · single token: 88 · 1+2+1: 29 (sum 9,000); cl100k gives 3+1 for all 9,000.
apply.hint: For the split pattern, map each id to len(enc.decode([i])) and collect the tuples in a collections.Counter.
